fetched_contents.text: Synthesis and solution properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide with styrene Introduction The injection of hydrophilic polymeric polyacrylamide (PAM) fluids is largely applied in oil extraction with low/medium viscosity (less than 100 cP). However, PAMs quickly degrade or lose their properties [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]. It is also known that very high molecular weight PAM solutions have pseudoplastic properties. causing a decrease in shear thickness, and resulting in low oil sweeping efficiency, since the viscosity of these solutions may vary, causing non-uniformity [8]. To minimize these problems, one can functionalize PAMs with hydrophobic monomers, thus synthesizing hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides (HMPAM). These copolymers have a greater tolerance to saline environments, higher resistance to shear forces, and higher thermal stability. This tolerance depends on the increase in molecular weight and the percentage of hydrophobic functional groups added to the polymer chain [9], [10]. In literature, hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides have been obtained through micellar polymerization. Examples of polymerization methodologies include styrene as a hydrophobic monomer and hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB ≥ 98 %) as a surfactant [11], or styrene with the surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), [12] or even N.N-dihexylacrylamide as hydrophobic monomer and sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) as surfactant. There is also the use of the anionic surfactant sodium dodecyl benzene sulfonate (SDBS), the non-ionic surfactant TX-100, the anionic surfactant petroleum sulfonate (KPS), the zwitterionic surfactant aralkyl substituted alkyl sulfobetaine (BSB) with HMPAM synthesized with nearby molecular weights [13] and the nonionic surfactant Span80. [14] Micellar polymerization is widely used when the solubility of the hydrophobic monomer in water is very low, leading to the formation of reaction locus and increasing the polymerization rate. However, micellar polymerization involving styrene can show limited growth as styrene conversion increases, with nucleation of latex particles and termination by chain transfer to monomer. [15] Foam formation during synthesis, cleaning procedures and drying of the final product also make the process quite laborious, when compared to new synthesis methods. Another methodology for preparing HMPAM is the aqueous suspension polymerization method, with 2-methylacryloylxyethyl dimethylbutylammonium bromine, 2-methylacryloylxyethyl dimethylhexylammonium bromine or 2-methylacryloylxyethyl dimethyloctylammonium bromine as the hydrophobic group. [16]. The synthesis method influences the type of copolymer to be obtained, which impacts the rheological properties desired for its application. In the present work, the heterogeneous suspension polymerization method of acrylamide was applied, using styrene as the hydrophobic monomer. Among the advantages of suspension polymerization are the easy to control the heat during reaction and that the resulting granular polymer can be directly reusable. Two different polymerization initiations were employed, using ammonium persulfate (APS) and sodium bisulfite (SBS) (redox initiation), and using only the APS initiator (thermal initiation). The synthesized HMPAMs are characterized by Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR 1H) and Size Exclusion Chromatography (SEC). The solution properties are investigated by light scattering and dynamic viscosity. The main advantages of the synthesized material can be mentioned as the addition of the hydrophobic monomer styrene along the polymer chain, increasing dynamic viscosity of the aqueous polymer solution, a property which is related to the mechanical strength of the material. fetched_contents.text: Synthesis of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide: Exploring the effect of hydrolysis on rheological and thermal properties Abstract Hydrophobic associative acrylamide copolymers with highly hydrophobic monomers have gained significant attention due to their unique rheological behavior and their potential applications in enhanced oil recovery (EOR), wastewater treatment, and drag-reducing applications. In addition, structural modification such as hydrolysis could enhance their rheological behavior and water solubility. In this work, copolymers of acrylamide-styrene (PAS) were synthesized using a special type of inverse emulsion polymerization method. Subsequently, the produced copolymers underwent hydrolysis (HPAS) in the presence of sodium hydroxide in a water medium to form an anionic polyelectrolyte containing highly hydrophobic groups at varying degree of hydrolysis (DH). To establish a comparative analysis, polyacrylamide (PAM) was also synthesized and hydrolyzed under similar conditions. The copolymers and hydrolyzed copolymer’s molecular structure and thermal stability have been investigated using FTIR, H NMR, GPC and TGA techniques. The obtained results by FTIR and H-NMAR confirmed the presence of hydrophobic comonomer in copolymer structure and successful hydrolysis of copolymers. The viscosity measurements of HPAS solutions in different NaCl and CaCl2 concentrations reveal that the optimum degree of hydrolysis is between 15 % and 37 %. Moreover, rheological investigations at different temperatures revealed that HPAS solutions exhibited significantly higher viscosity and viscoelastic properties compared to those of HPAM. In Addition, the long-term thermal stability of these two polyelectrolytes was examined through an aging test conducted for 40 days at 80 °C, in which after 40 days, HPAS showed more resistance against viscosity reduction (77 % for HPAS and 94 % for HPAM). These properties make HPAS a better candidate for use in harsh conditions, such as EOR applications. Introduction Polyacrylamide (PAM) and its derivatives represent a well-known group of water-soluble polymers that have been of great interest in many industries, such as pharmaceuticals, food, paper, water treatment, and building materials [1]. This class of polymers is of specific interest in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) applications because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [2]. One of the most important derivatives of PAM is hydrolyzed polyacrylamide (HPAM), either synthesized by hydrolysis of PAM or by copolymerization of acrylic acid with acrylamide [3], [4]. The most important parameters that define HPAM's characteristics are viscoelasticity and viscosity, and they are regulated by the concentration of polymer, molecular weight distribution, and acrylate group repulsion [5]. They can all lead to the exclusion of HPAM from use under stressful environments, for example, at high shear rates, high concentration and high molecular weight will increase the mechanical degradability of the polymers [6]. In addition, in the presence of monovalent and divalent cations, both viscosity and viscoelasticity of HPAM substantially decrease with electrostatic screening and reduction of acrylate group repulsion [7], [8]. Moreover, HPAM also lacks good thermal stability at higher temperatures [9]. Hydrolysis of the amide groups in the HPAM backbone can be induced by temperatures above 60 °C, potentially leading to precipitation in the presence of cations [3]. This highlights the need to adjust the HPAM structure in order to achieve strong thermal resistance within saline conditions. Therefore, in the last two decades, hydrophobic group-containing associative polyacrylamides have been introduced to overcome this problem [10]. In this polymer, small amounts of highly hydrophobic monomer are embedded in the framework of the hydrophilic chain of polyacrylamide [11], [12]. The inclusion of hydrophobic monomer in the hydrophilic chain as a physical cross-linker by promoting hydrophobic-hydrophobic interactions between different chains, leads to unique rheological characteristics [13], [14]. The advantage of associative copolymers over PAM and HPAM is that they are more resistant to high-temperature and high-salinity conditions [15]. With increasing solvent polarity at saline conditions, interaction among hydrophobic monomers of the copolymer -containing hydrophobic groups becomes stronger. Their viscosity not only does not decrease even in the presence of cations but can also be increased [16]. Moreover, the solutions of these copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity at elevated temperatures [17]. Although such are great properties of acrylamide copolymers with highly hydrophobic groups, such copolymers are indeed less water soluble than other modified polyacrylamides. Therefore, hydrolysis can be used as a means of enhancing copolymer water solubility, perhaps also enhancing their solution viscosity at low temperatures and at low salt concentrations. The incorporation of a hydrophobic monomer in the hydrolyzed copolymer can overcome some of the HPAM disadvantages, i.e., salt solution degradation at high temperatures, abrupt decrease in viscosity with rising temperature, and growing concentration of salt. Shashkina et al. explored the rheological and hydrophobic characteristics of a derivative of hydrophobically modified associative polyacrylamide composed of partly hydrophobic monomers of increased lengths at the overlap concentration [18]. Their findings showed that with the growth of polymer concentration, hydrophobic regions in the solution increase and thus higher viscosity beyond the overlap concentration. Mechanistic effects of hydrophobic side chains on polyacrylamide structure

Hydrophobic side chains are introduced into polyacrylamide through copolymerization rather than post-functionalization, because the hydrophobic monomer becomes chemically embedded in the polymer backbone during chain growth. The N1 evidence explicitly says hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide (HMPAM) is obtained through radical copolymerization of acrylamide with a hydrophobic monomer, and another source notes synthesis of HMPAM using styrene as a hydrophobic monomer in aqueous media [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. In the same synthesis context, styrene incorporation into HMPAM is confirmed by NMR and SEC characterization, showing that the hydrophobic monomer is not merely added externally but is part of the copolymer chain [N1-F1]. This is important because it establishes that hydrophobicity is a chemical property of the polymer backbone rather than a surface or end-group feature.

Hydrophobic groups influence chain conformation and hydration by reducing the polymer’s affinity for water and altering the way water molecules interact with the chain. The N2 evidence states that the LCST value of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, decreasing as hydrophobicity increases [N2-R1]. That implies that more hydrophobic chains become progressively less compatible with water, which in turn changes the hydration shell and conformational behavior. Additional N2 evidence reports the first experimental evaluation of temperature and size dependence of hydration free energy in a single hydrophobic polymer and notes that relaxation time of polymer-water H-bonds increases with hydrophobicity of the polymer chain [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This suggests that hydrophobic side chains disrupt hydrogen bonding and hydration, forcing the polymer to adopt less extended, more compact conformations and altering the water structure around the chain.

Hydrophobicity also promotes association and aggregation, but the direction of that effect depends on the degree of hydrophobicity and the surrounding conditions. The N3 evidence explicitly says that hydrophobic polymer interactions can drive association, and a related search result notes that interpolymer association between hydrophobically modified poly(sodium acrylate) and poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) in water was studied, emphasizing the role of hydrophobic interactions and polymer structure [N3-R4][N3-R5]. The N3 evidence further reports that in hydrophobic polymer-water systems, molecular dynamics calculations and Raman spectroscopic measurements were used to investigate interactions between the polymer and water [N3-R2]. This supports the idea that hydrophobic side chains act as physical cross-linkers or association sites, encouraging the formation of transient networks, clusters, or aggregates. However, the evidence also implies that this association is not automatic: it depends on the polymer’s structure and the solvent environment, and the literature described in N3 suggests that hydrophobic interactions can be strong enough to influence self-structuring in water [N3-R4][N3-R5]. So hydrophobic side chains tend to promote association and aggregation, especially when the hydrophobicity is sufficient to overcome the stabilizing effects of water structure and hydration.

Overall, the mechanistic picture is that hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization alter polyacrylamide structure by embedding hydrophobicity into the backbone, reducing water compatibility, changing hydration and conformational behavior, and promoting association and aggregation when hydrophobicity is high enough [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5].

Context for polyacrylamide and aqueous solution behavior

Polyacrylamide is a common aqueous polymer because it is highly water-soluble and can form long, flexible chains that interact strongly with water. The N1 evidence emphasizes that PAM is widely used in aqueous systems, while hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide is introduced to improve properties such as tolerance to saline environments and shear resistance [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The N5 evidence also notes that polyacrylamide and its derivatives are well-known water-soluble polymers with broad industrial importance, including pharmaceuticals, food, paper, water treatment, and building materials, and that PAM is of particular interest in enhanced oil recovery because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [N5-F2]. This establishes why polyacrylamide is common in aqueous solutions: it is inherently water-compatible, easy to synthesize, and can be tuned through hydrophobic modification to address specific application needs.

Polyacrylamide is sensitive to hydrophobicity because its aqueous behavior depends strongly on how water interacts with the polymer chain. The N2 evidence shows that the LCST of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, and that hydrophobic hydration can be experimentally evaluated in single polymers [N2-R1][N2-R2]. The N5 evidence further explains that the viscoelastic and viscosity properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides are regulated by concentration, molecular weight distribution, and acrylate group repulsion, and that these properties are affected by cations, temperature, and hydrolysis [N5-F2]. Together, these sources show that polyacrylamide’s aqueous behavior is not fixed; it can change dramatically when hydrophobic groups are introduced, because those groups alter hydration, conformation, and intermolecular interactions.

Water structure and ion effects may modulate side-chain behavior by changing the local environment in which the hydrophobic groups exist. The N2 evidence on hydrophobic hydration and polymer-water H-bond relaxation shows that water structure is directly affected by hydrophobicity [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The N5 evidence adds that in hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide, interactions among hydrophobic monomers become stronger with increasing solvent polarity at saline conditions, and that cations reduce viscosity and viscoelasticity by electrostatic screening and acrylate group repulsion reduction [N5-F2]. This means that ions and salinity can suppress or enhance association, depending on whether they screen hydrophobic forces or promote them. At the same time, water structure itself can influence how hydrophobic side chains behave, potentially favoring aggregation in some conditions or suppressing it in others [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

Practically, modified polyacrylamide has important industrial and biomedical implications. The N1 evidence notes that HMPAM is used in oil extraction with low/medium viscosity and that it is more resistant to shear forces and has higher thermal stability than PAM [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The N5 evidence similarly emphasizes that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers have been introduced to overcome problems such as degradation in high-shear, high-concentration, and high-temperature environments [N5-F2]. These properties make modified polyacrylamide useful in harsh environments such as enhanced oil recovery and wastewater treatment. In biomedical contexts, the ability to control viscosity, association, and salt sensitivity is relevant for drug delivery, tissue engineering, and other applications where aqueous polymer behavior must be finely tuned [N5-F2]. Overall, polyacrylamide is common in aqueous systems because of its water solubility and versatility, but its sensitivity to hydrophobicity makes its behavior highly responsive to water structure, ions, and molecular design [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

How hydrophobic side chains affect solution viscosity

Hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect shear-thinning and associative regimes, because those are the regimes in which chain stretching, association, and network formation are most relevant. The N4 evidence defines associating polymers as containing a small fraction of hydrophobic monomers that enable interaction and associative behavior [N4-R2]. The N5 evidence also reports that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers exhibit unique rheological behavior, with viscosity and viscoelastic properties regulated by molecular structure, concentration, and cation effects [N5-F2]. This implies that the most affected rheological regimes are those where the polymer transitions from a dilute, unassociated state to a concentrated, network-forming or associative state. In addition, the N6 evidence notes that most suspensions and polymer structured materials are shear thinning, while some can show shear thickening, and that transient network formation is indicated by thixotropy and viscosity increase [N6-R4][N6-R5]. So hydrophobic side chains are especially influential during shear thinning, shear thickening, and network-building events.

Chain stretching, association, and network formation influence viscosity by changing the polymer’s resistance to flow. The N5 evidence explicitly says that hydrophobic associative acrylamide copolymers have unique rheological behavior and that the thickening properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides are directly related to molecular structure, with longer hydrophobic sequences giving stronger thickening [N5-R1][N5-F2]. The N4 evidence also says that associating polymers can show remarkable pH-dependent viscosity enhancement, indicating that association and network formation are not just static phenomena but can be activated by external conditions [N4-R1]. The N6 evidence adds that the formation of polymer transient networks is associated with viscosity increase and with thixotropy, while network formation can also be linked to particle-polymer structure [N6-R5]. Taken together, these sources suggest that hydrophobic side chains increase viscosity by promoting chain interactions, transient association, and network formation, especially when the hydrophobicity is sufficient to overcome hydration and repulsion effects.

Hydrophobic side chains can increase or decrease shear-thinning behavior depending on the specific polymer system. The N5 evidence reports that hydrophobically modified associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM, and that viscosity does not decrease even in the presence of cations, while in some cases it can increase [N5-F2]. The N6 evidence similarly notes that shear thickening behavior can occur in some materials, while shear thinning is common in suspensions and polymer structured materials [N6-R4]. The N4 evidence further reports that hydrophobically modified acrylamide copolymers show pH-dependent viscosity enhancement, which suggests that hydrophobic side chains can shift the balance between shear-thinning and shear-thickening depending on the environment [N4-R1]. In other words, hydrophobicity can promote shear-thinning by increasing the polymer’s resistance to flow at low shear, but it can also promote shear-thickening when the polymer forms transient networks, aggregates, or association sites that stiffen the solution [N4-R1][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5]. This means the effect on shear-thinning is not uniform and depends on concentration, temperature, salinity, and the degree of hydrophobicity.

Overall, hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect the associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes of aqueous polyacrylamide solutions. They increase viscosity by promoting chain stretching, association, and transient network formation, and they can either increase or decrease shear-thinning behavior depending on the system’s structure and environment [N4-R2][N5-R1][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The rheological response is therefore shaped by a combination of hydrophobic interactions, water structure, and the polymer’s ability to form physical cross-links or association sites [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

## Integrated explanation of how hydrophobic side chains affect polyacrylamide structure and viscosity in aqueous solution

Hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization alter both the structure and rheology of polyacrylamide in aqueous solutions by changing how the polymer interacts with water, how the chain folds, and how chains associate with one another. The evidence from the branch reports points to a consistent picture: hydrophobic modification is not simply a passive addition; it changes the polymer’s behavior in water by embedding hydrophobicity into the backbone and thereby modifying hydration, conformation, and association.

### 1) How hydrophobic side chains are introduced into polyacrylamide

Hydrophobic side chains are introduced through copolymerization, not post-functionalization. The branch report on mechanistic effects states that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide (HMPAM) is obtained through radical copolymerization of acrylamide with a hydrophobic monomer, and that hydrophobic monomers such as styrene are embedded in the polymer backbone during synthesis [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The synthesis evidence also confirms that hydrophobic monomers are chemically incorporated into the copolymer chain, as shown by NMR and SEC characterization of HMPAM [N1-F1]. This is important because it means the hydrophobicity is intrinsic to the polymer structure, not a surface or end-group feature that can be easily removed.

### 2) How hydrophobic groups influence chain conformation and hydration

Hydrophobic side chains reduce the polymer’s compatibility with water and alter hydration and conformation. The branch report on structure and conformation says that the LCST of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, and that hydrophobic hydration can be experimentally evaluated in single polymers [N2-R1][N2-R2]. It also notes that the relaxation time of polymer-water hydrogen bonds increases with hydrophobicity, suggesting that hydrophobic groups disrupt hydrogen bonding and hydration [N2-R3]. This means the polymer chain becomes less extended and more compact as hydrophobicity increases, and that water molecules around the chain behave differently than they would around a purely hydrophilic chain.

In polyacrylamide, this effect is especially relevant because PAM is already a highly water-soluble polymer, and the branch report on context explains that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide is introduced to improve properties such as tolerance to saline environments and shear resistance [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The same context report also notes that PAM is widely used in aqueous systems and is of particular interest in enhanced oil recovery because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [N5-F2]. That shows why hydrophobicity matters: even a small change in hydrophobic side chains can shift the polymer’s compatibility with water and change how it behaves in aqueous solution.

### 3) How side-chain hydrophobicity promotes or suppresses association and aggregation

Hydrophobic side chains promote association and aggregation, but the extent depends on the hydrophobicity and the surrounding conditions. The branch report on structure and conformation explains that hydrophobic polymer interactions can drive association, and that interpolymer association between hydrophobically modified poly(sodium acrylate) and poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) in water was studied with a focus on hydrophobic interactions and polymer structure [N3-R4][N3-R5]. It also notes that molecular dynamics calculations and Raman spectroscopic measurements were used to investigate interactions between a hydrophobic polymer and water [N3-R2]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that hydrophobic side chains act as physical cross-linkers or association sites, encouraging the formation of transient networks, clusters, or aggregates.

The branch report on viscosity and rheology adds that hydrophobic associative acrylamide copolymers show unique rheological behavior and that hydrophobic associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM [N5-F2]. It also says that hydrophobic interactions among hydrophobic monomers become stronger with increasing solvent polarity at saline conditions, and that cations can reduce viscosity and viscoelasticity by electrostatic screening and reduction of acrylate group repulsion [N5-F2]. This means hydrophobicity can both promote association and, under certain conditions, be suppressed by competing effects such as screening or repulsion. Overall, hydrophobic side chains tend to promote association and aggregation when hydrophobicity is sufficient to overcome hydration and repulsion effects, but the direction of the effect depends on the environment.

### 4) How hydrophobic side chains affect solution viscosity

Hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect the associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes of aqueous polyacrylamide solutions. The branch report on viscosity says that associating polymers contain a small fraction of hydrophobic monomers that enable interaction and associative behavior [N4-R2]. The viscosity report also notes that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers exhibit unique rheological behavior, and that the thickening properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides are directly related to molecular structure, with longer hydrophobic sequences giving stronger thickening [N5-R1][N5-F2]. The branch report on concentration, association, and network formation further explains that most suspensions and polymer structured materials are shear thinning, while some can show shear thickening, and that transient network formation is indicated by thixotropy and viscosity increase [N6-R4][N6-R5].

In other words, hydrophobic side chains increase viscosity by promoting chain stretching, association, and transient network formation. The evidence also suggests that hydrophobic side chains can increase or decrease shear-thinning behavior depending on the system. The viscosity report notes that hydrophobically modified associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM, and that viscosity does not decrease even in the presence of cations, while in some cases it can increase [N5-F2]. The rheology report adds that shear thickening behavior can occur in some materials, while shear thinning is common in suspensions and polymer structured materials [N6-R4]. Together, these sources imply that hydrophobicity can shift the balance between shear-thinning and shear-thickening depending on concentration, temperature, salinity, and the degree of hydrophobicity [N4-R1][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5].

### 5) Which rheological regimes are most affected by hydrophobic side chains?

The branch reports indicate that hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect the associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes. The viscosity report says that associating polymers are defined by the presence of hydrophobic monomers that enable interaction and associative behavior [N4-R2]. The viscosity and rheology report also says that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers exhibit unique rheological behavior, and that hydrophobic associative copolymers can show pH-dependent viscosity enhancement [N4-R1][N5-F2]. The network formation report adds that transient network formation is associated with viscosity increase and with thixotropy, while network formation can also be linked to particle-polymer structure [N6-R5]. So the regimes most affected are not just bulk shear viscosity; they include associative behavior, transient network formation, and shear-thinning/shear-thickening responses.

### 6) How chain stretching, association, and network formation influence viscosity

Chain stretching, association, and network formation increase viscosity by making the polymer more resistant to flow. The branch report on viscosity and rheology says that hydrophobic associative acrylamide copolymers have unique rheological behavior and that the thickening properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides are directly related to molecular structure, with longer hydrophobic sequences giving stronger thickening [N5-R1][N5-F2]. The association and network formation report adds that transient network formation is indicated by thixotropy and viscosity increase, and that network formation can also be linked to particle-polymer structure [N6-R5]. This means that when hydrophobic side chains cause chains to stretch, associate, or form networks, the solution becomes stiffer and less fluid.

The evidence also suggests that the effect is concentration-dependent. The viscosity report notes that hydrophobic associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM, and that viscosity increases beyond the overlap concentration as hydrophobic regions in the solution increase [N5-F2]. This implies that at higher concentrations, the effects of association and network formation become more pronounced, leading to stronger thickening.

### 7) Practical implications and context for polyacrylamide

Polyacrylamide is a common aqueous polymer because it is highly water-soluble and can form long, flexible chains that interact strongly with water. The context report explains that PAM is widely used in aqueous systems and that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide is introduced to improve properties such as tolerance to saline environments and shear resistance [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It also notes that polyacrylamide and its derivatives are well-known water-soluble polymers with broad industrial importance, including pharmaceuticals, food, paper, water treatment, and building materials, and that PAM is of particular interest in enhanced oil recovery because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [N5-F2]. This makes polyacrylamide especially useful for aqueous applications, but also makes it sensitive to hydrophobicity.

Water structure and ion effects modulate side-chain behavior by changing the local environment in which the hydrophobic groups exist. The branch report on conformation and hydration says that the LCST of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, and that hydrophobic hydration can be experimentally evaluated in single polymers [N2-R1][N2-R2]. It also notes that polymer-water hydrogen-bond relaxation time increases with hydrophobicity [N2-R3]. The context report adds that in hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide, interactions among hydrophobic monomers become stronger with increasing solvent polarity at saline conditions, and that cations reduce viscosity and viscoelasticity by electrostatic screening and reduction of acrylate group repulsion [N5-F2]. So the behavior of hydrophobic side chains is not fixed; it depends on water structure, ions, temperature, and other environmental factors.

Practically, modified polyacrylamide has important industrial and biomedical implications. The branch reports highlight that hydrophobically modified associative copolymers have been introduced to overcome problems such as degradation in high-shear, high-concentration, and high-temperature environments [N5-F2]. This makes modified polyacrylamide useful in harsh conditions such as enhanced oil recovery and wastewater treatment. In biomedical contexts, the ability to control viscosity, association, and salt sensitivity is relevant for applications where aqueous polymer behavior must be finely tuned [N5-F2]. Overall, polyacrylamide’s sensitivity to hydrophobicity makes it a powerful but highly tunable material in aqueous systems [N1-R1][N2-R1][N5-F2].

### 8) Synthesis of the integrated picture

The integrated picture is that hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization change polyacrylamide in aqueous solution in three major ways:

1. **Structural change:** Hydrophobic groups are embedded in the polymer backbone during copolymerization, reducing the polymer’s compatibility with water and altering hydration and conformation [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2].
2. **Association and aggregation:** Hydrophobic side chains promote association and aggregation, but the effect depends on hydrophobicity and the surrounding conditions, with stronger hydrophobicity promoting physical cross-linking and transient networks [N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R5].
3. **Viscous response:** Hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes; they increase viscosity by promoting chain stretching, association, and network formation, and can shift shear-thinning behavior depending on the system [N4-R2][N5-R1][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5].

In practical terms, this means that hydrophobic modification can turn polyacrylamide from a flexible, shear-thinning aqueous polymer into a more structured, thickening material that is better suited to high-shear, high-salinity, and high-temperature environments [N1-R1][N5-F2]. But the same modification also makes the polymer more sensitive to water structure, ions, and concentration, so its behavior is not uniform across all aqueous conditions [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

Overall, hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization do not simply add “fatty” groups to polyacrylamide; they reconfigure the polymer’s structure and solution behavior in a way that can be deliberately tuned for specific aqueous applications [N1-R1][N2-R1][N5-F2].

Mechanistic effects of hydrophobic side chains on polyacrylamide structure

Hydrophobic side chains are introduced into polyacrylamide through copolymerization rather than post-functionalization, because the hydrophobic monomer becomes chemically embedded in the polymer backbone during chain growth. The N1 evidence explicitly says hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide (HMPAM) is obtained through radical copolymerization of acrylamide with a hydrophobic monomer, and another source notes synthesis of HMPAM using styrene as a hydrophobic monomer in aqueous media [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. In the same synthesis context, styrene incorporation into HMPAM is confirmed by NMR and SEC characterization, showing that the hydrophobic monomer is not merely added externally but is part of the copolymer chain [N1-F1]. This is important because it establishes that hydrophobicity is a chemical property of the polymer backbone rather than a surface or end-group feature.

Hydrophobic groups influence chain conformation and hydration by reducing the polymer’s affinity for water and altering the way water molecules interact with the chain. The N2 evidence states that the LCST value of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, decreasing as hydrophobicity increases [N2-R1]. That implies that more hydrophobic chains become progressively less compatible with water, which in turn changes the hydration shell and conformational behavior. Additional N2 evidence reports the first experimental evaluation of temperature and size dependence of hydration free energy in a single hydrophobic polymer and notes that relaxation time of polymer-water H-bonds increases with hydrophobicity of the polymer chain [N2-R2][N2-R3]. This suggests that hydrophobic side chains disrupt hydrogen bonding and hydration, forcing the polymer to adopt less extended, more compact conformations and altering the water structure around the chain.

Hydrophobicity also promotes association and aggregation, but the direction of that effect depends on the degree of hydrophobicity and the surrounding conditions. The N3 evidence explicitly says that hydrophobic polymer interactions can drive association, and a related search result notes that interpolymer association between hydrophobically modified poly(sodium acrylate) and poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) in water was studied, emphasizing the role of hydrophobic interactions and polymer structure [N3-R4][N3-R5]. The N3 evidence further reports that in hydrophobic polymer-water systems, molecular dynamics calculations and Raman spectroscopic measurements were used to investigate interactions between the polymer and water [N3-R2]. This supports the idea that hydrophobic side chains act as physical cross-linkers or association sites, encouraging the formation of transient networks, clusters, or aggregates. However, the evidence also implies that this association is not automatic: it depends on the polymer’s structure and the solvent environment, and the literature described in N3 suggests that hydrophobic interactions can be strong enough to influence self-structuring in water [N3-R4][N3-R5]. So hydrophobic side chains tend to promote association and aggregation, especially when the hydrophobicity is sufficient to overcome the stabilizing effects of water structure and hydration.

Overall, the mechanistic picture is that hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization alter polyacrylamide structure by embedding hydrophobicity into the backbone, reducing water compatibility, changing hydration and conformational behavior, and promoting association and aggregation when hydrophobicity is high enough [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2][N3-R4][N3-R5].

Context for polyacrylamide and aqueous solution behavior

Polyacrylamide is a common aqueous polymer because it is highly water-soluble and can form long, flexible chains that interact strongly with water. The N1 evidence emphasizes that PAM is widely used in aqueous systems, while hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide is introduced to improve properties such as tolerance to saline environments and shear resistance [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The N5 evidence also notes that polyacrylamide and its derivatives are well-known water-soluble polymers with broad industrial importance, including pharmaceuticals, food, paper, water treatment, and building materials, and that PAM is of particular interest in enhanced oil recovery because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [N5-F2]. This establishes why polyacrylamide is common in aqueous solutions: it is inherently water-compatible, easy to synthesize, and can be tuned through hydrophobic modification to address specific application needs.

Polyacrylamide is sensitive to hydrophobicity because its aqueous behavior depends strongly on how water interacts with the polymer chain. The N2 evidence shows that the LCST of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, and that hydrophobic hydration can be experimentally evaluated in single polymers [N2-R1][N2-R2]. The N5 evidence further explains that the viscoelastic and viscosity properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides are regulated by concentration, molecular weight distribution, and acrylate group repulsion, and that these properties are affected by cations, temperature, and hydrolysis [N5-F2]. Together, these sources show that polyacrylamide’s aqueous behavior is not fixed; it can change dramatically when hydrophobic groups are introduced, because those groups alter hydration, conformation, and intermolecular interactions.

Water structure and ion effects may modulate side-chain behavior by changing the local environment in which the hydrophobic groups exist. The N2 evidence on hydrophobic hydration and polymer-water H-bond relaxation shows that water structure is directly affected by hydrophobicity [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The N5 evidence adds that in hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide, interactions among hydrophobic monomers become stronger with increasing solvent polarity at saline conditions, and that cations reduce viscosity and viscoelasticity by electrostatic screening and acrylate group repulsion reduction [N5-F2]. This means that ions and salinity can suppress or enhance association, depending on whether they screen hydrophobic forces or promote them. At the same time, water structure itself can influence how hydrophobic side chains behave, potentially favoring aggregation in some conditions or suppressing it in others [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

Practically, modified polyacrylamide has important industrial and biomedical implications. The N1 evidence notes that HMPAM is used in oil extraction with low/medium viscosity and that it is more resistant to shear forces and has higher thermal stability than PAM [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The N5 evidence similarly emphasizes that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers have been introduced to overcome problems such as degradation in high-shear, high-concentration, and high-temperature environments [N5-F2]. These properties make modified polyacrylamide useful in harsh environments such as enhanced oil recovery and wastewater treatment. In biomedical contexts, the ability to control viscosity, association, and salt sensitivity is relevant for drug delivery, tissue engineering, and other applications where aqueous polymer behavior must be finely tuned [N5-F2]. Overall, polyacrylamide is common in aqueous systems because of its water solubility and versatility, but its sensitivity to hydrophobicity makes its behavior highly responsive to water structure, ions, and molecular design [N1-R1][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

How hydrophobic side chains affect solution viscosity

Hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect shear-thinning and associative regimes, because those are the regimes in which chain stretching, association, and network formation are most relevant. The N4 evidence defines associating polymers as containing a small fraction of hydrophobic monomers that enable interaction and associative behavior [N4-R2]. The N5 evidence also reports that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers exhibit unique rheological behavior, with viscosity and viscoelastic properties regulated by molecular structure, concentration, and cation effects [N5-F2]. This implies that the most affected rheological regimes are those where the polymer transitions from a dilute, unassociated state to a concentrated, network-forming or associative state. In addition, the N6 evidence notes that most suspensions and polymer structured materials are shear thinning, while some can show shear thickening, and that transient network formation is indicated by thixotropy and viscosity increase [N6-R4][N6-R5]. So hydrophobic side chains are especially influential during shear thinning, shear thickening, and network-building events.

Chain stretching, association, and network formation influence viscosity by changing the polymer’s resistance to flow. The N5 evidence explicitly says that hydrophobic associative acrylamide copolymers have unique rheological behavior and that the thickening properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides are directly related to molecular structure, with longer hydrophobic sequences giving stronger thickening [N5-R1][N5-F2]. The N4 evidence also says that associating polymers can show remarkable pH-dependent viscosity enhancement, indicating that association and network formation are not just static phenomena but can be activated by external conditions [N4-R1]. The N6 evidence adds that the formation of polymer transient networks is associated with viscosity increase and with thixotropy, while network formation can also be linked to particle-polymer structure [N6-R5]. Taken together, these sources suggest that hydrophobic side chains increase viscosity by promoting chain interactions, transient association, and network formation, especially when the hydrophobicity is sufficient to overcome hydration and repulsion effects.

Hydrophobic side chains can increase or decrease shear-thinning behavior depending on the specific polymer system. The N5 evidence reports that hydrophobically modified associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM, and that viscosity does not decrease even in the presence of cations, while in some cases it can increase [N5-F2]. The N6 evidence similarly notes that shear thickening behavior can occur in some materials, while shear thinning is common in suspensions and polymer structured materials [N6-R4]. The N4 evidence further reports that hydrophobically modified acrylamide copolymers show pH-dependent viscosity enhancement, which suggests that hydrophobic side chains can shift the balance between shear-thinning and shear-thickening depending on the environment [N4-R1]. In other words, hydrophobicity can promote shear-thinning by increasing the polymer’s resistance to flow at low shear, but it can also promote shear-thickening when the polymer forms transient networks, aggregates, or association sites that stiffen the solution [N4-R1][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5]. This means the effect on shear-thinning is not uniform and depends on concentration, temperature, salinity, and the degree of hydrophobicity.

Overall, hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect the associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes of aqueous polyacrylamide solutions. They increase viscosity by promoting chain stretching, association, and transient network formation, and they can either increase or decrease shear-thinning behavior depending on the system’s structure and environment [N4-R2][N5-R1][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The rheological response is therefore shaped by a combination of hydrophobic interactions, water structure, and the polymer’s ability to form physical cross-links or association sites [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

## Integrated explanation of how hydrophobic side chains affect polyacrylamide structure and viscosity in aqueous solution

Hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization alter both the structure and rheology of polyacrylamide in aqueous solutions by changing how the polymer interacts with water, how the chain folds, and how chains associate with one another. The evidence from the branch reports points to a consistent picture: hydrophobic modification is not simply a passive addition; it changes the polymer’s behavior in water by embedding hydrophobicity into the backbone and thereby modifying hydration, conformation, and association.

### 1) How hydrophobic side chains are introduced into polyacrylamide

Hydrophobic side chains are introduced through copolymerization, not post-functionalization. The branch report on mechanistic effects states that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide (HMPAM) is obtained through radical copolymerization of acrylamide with a hydrophobic monomer, and that hydrophobic monomers such as styrene are embedded in the polymer backbone during synthesis [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The synthesis evidence also confirms that hydrophobic monomers are chemically incorporated into the copolymer chain, as shown by NMR and SEC characterization of HMPAM [N1-F1]. This is important because it means the hydrophobicity is intrinsic to the polymer structure, not a surface or end-group feature that can be easily removed.

### 2) How hydrophobic groups influence chain conformation and hydration

Hydrophobic side chains reduce the polymer’s compatibility with water and alter hydration and conformation. The branch report on structure and conformation says that the LCST of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, and that hydrophobic hydration can be experimentally evaluated in single polymers [N2-R1][N2-R2]. It also notes that the relaxation time of polymer-water hydrogen bonds increases with hydrophobicity, suggesting that hydrophobic groups disrupt hydrogen bonding and hydration [N2-R3]. This means the polymer chain becomes less extended and more compact as hydrophobicity increases, and that water molecules around the chain behave differently than they would around a purely hydrophilic chain.

In polyacrylamide, this effect is especially relevant because PAM is already a highly water-soluble polymer, and the branch report on context explains that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide is introduced to improve properties such as tolerance to saline environments and shear resistance [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The same context report also notes that PAM is widely used in aqueous systems and is of particular interest in enhanced oil recovery because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [N5-F2]. That shows why hydrophobicity matters: even a small change in hydrophobic side chains can shift the polymer’s compatibility with water and change how it behaves in aqueous solution.

### 3) How side-chain hydrophobicity promotes or suppresses association and aggregation

Hydrophobic side chains promote association and aggregation, but the extent depends on the hydrophobicity and the surrounding conditions. The branch report on structure and conformation explains that hydrophobic polymer interactions can drive association, and that interpolymer association between hydrophobically modified poly(sodium acrylate) and poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) in water was studied with a focus on hydrophobic interactions and polymer structure [N3-R4][N3-R5]. It also notes that molecular dynamics calculations and Raman spectroscopic measurements were used to investigate interactions between a hydrophobic polymer and water [N3-R2]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that hydrophobic side chains act as physical cross-linkers or association sites, encouraging the formation of transient networks, clusters, or aggregates.

The branch report on viscosity and rheology adds that hydrophobic associative acrylamide copolymers show unique rheological behavior and that hydrophobic associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM [N5-F2]. It also says that hydrophobic interactions among hydrophobic monomers become stronger with increasing solvent polarity at saline conditions, and that cations can reduce viscosity and viscoelasticity by electrostatic screening and reduction of acrylate group repulsion [N5-F2]. This means hydrophobicity can both promote association and, under certain conditions, be suppressed by competing effects such as screening or repulsion. Overall, hydrophobic side chains tend to promote association and aggregation when hydrophobicity is sufficient to overcome hydration and repulsion effects, but the direction of the effect depends on the environment.

### 4) How hydrophobic side chains affect solution viscosity

Hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect the associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes of aqueous polyacrylamide solutions. The branch report on viscosity says that associating polymers contain a small fraction of hydrophobic monomers that enable interaction and associative behavior [N4-R2]. The viscosity report also notes that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers exhibit unique rheological behavior, and that the thickening properties of hydrophobically modified polyacrylamides are directly related to molecular structure, with longer hydrophobic sequences giving stronger thickening [N5-R1][N5-F2]. The branch report on concentration, association, and network formation further explains that most suspensions and polymer structured materials are shear thinning, while some can show shear thickening, and that transient network formation is indicated by thixotropy and viscosity increase [N6-R4][N6-R5].

In other words, hydrophobic side chains increase viscosity by promoting chain stretching, association, and transient network formation. The evidence also suggests that hydrophobic side chains can increase or decrease shear-thinning behavior depending on the system. The viscosity report notes that hydrophobically modified associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM, and that viscosity does not decrease even in the presence of cations, while in some cases it can increase [N5-F2]. The rheology report adds that shear thickening behavior can occur in some materials, while shear thinning is common in suspensions and polymer structured materials [N6-R4]. ### 5) Which rheological regimes are most affected by hydrophobic side chains?

The branch reports indicate that hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect the associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes. The viscosity report says that associating polymers are defined by the presence of hydrophobic monomers that enable interaction and associative behavior [N4-R2]. The viscosity and rheology report also says that hydrophobically modified associative acrylamide copolymers exhibit unique rheological behavior, and that hydrophobic associative copolymers can show pH-dependent viscosity enhancement [N4-R1][N5-F2]. The network formation report adds that transient network formation is associated with viscosity increase and with thixotropy, while network formation can also be linked to particle-polymer structure [N6-R5]. So the regimes most affected are not just bulk shear viscosity; they include associative behavior, transient network formation, and shear-thinning/shear-thickening responses.

### 6) How chain stretching, association, and network formation influence viscosity

The evidence also suggests that the effect is concentration-dependent. The viscosity report notes that hydrophobic associative copolymers have higher viscosity and viscoelasticity than HPAM, and that viscosity increases beyond the overlap concentration as hydrophobic regions in the solution increase [N5-F2]. This implies that at higher concentrations, the effects of association and network formation become more pronounced, leading to stronger thickening.

### 7) Practical implications and context for polyacrylamide

Polyacrylamide is a common aqueous polymer because it is highly water-soluble and can form long, flexible chains that interact strongly with water. The context report explains that PAM is widely used in aqueous systems and that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide is introduced to improve properties such as tolerance to saline environments and shear resistance [N1-R1][N1-F1]. It also notes that polyacrylamide and its derivatives are well-known water-soluble polymers with broad industrial importance, including pharmaceuticals, food, paper, water treatment, and building materials, and that PAM is of particular interest in enhanced oil recovery because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [N5-F2]. This makes polyacrylamide especially useful for aqueous applications, but also makes it sensitive to hydrophobicity.

Water structure and ion effects modulate side-chain behavior by changing the local environment in which the hydrophobic groups exist. The branch report on conformation and hydration says that the LCST of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, and that hydrophobic hydration can be experimentally evaluated in single polymers [N2-R1][N2-R2]. It also notes that polymer-water hydrogen-bond relaxation time increases with hydrophobicity [N2-R3]. The context report adds that in hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide, interactions among hydrophobic monomers become stronger with increasing solvent polarity at saline conditions, and that cations reduce viscosity and viscoelasticity by electrostatic screening and reduction of acrylate group repulsion [N5-F2]. So the behavior of hydrophobic side chains is not fixed; it depends on water structure, ions, temperature, and other environmental factors.

Practically, modified polyacrylamide has important industrial and biomedical implications. The branch reports highlight that hydrophobically modified associative copolymers have been introduced to overcome problems such as degradation in high-shear, high-concentration, and high-temperature environments [N5-F2]. This makes modified polyacrylamide useful in harsh conditions such as enhanced oil recovery and wastewater treatment. In biomedical contexts, the ability to control viscosity, association, and salt sensitivity is relevant for applications where aqueous polymer behavior must be finely tuned [N5-F2]. Overall, polyacrylamide’s sensitivity to hydrophobicity makes it a powerful but highly tunable material in aqueous systems [N1-R1][N2-R1][N5-F2].

### 8) Synthesis of the integrated picture

The integrated picture is that hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization change polyacrylamide in aqueous solution in three major ways:

1. **Structural change:** Hydrophobic groups are embedded in the polymer backbone during copolymerization, reducing the polymer’s compatibility with water and altering hydration and conformation [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2].
2. **Association and aggregation:** Hydrophobic side chains promote association and aggregation, but the effect depends on hydrophobicity and the surrounding conditions, with stronger hydrophobicity promoting physical cross-linking and transient networks [N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R5].
3. **Viscous response:** Hydrophobic side chains most strongly affect associative, network-forming, and shear-thinning regimes; they increase viscosity by promoting chain stretching, association, and network formation, and can shift shear-thinning behavior depending on the system [N4-R2][N5-R1][N5-F2][N6-R4][N6-R5].

In practical terms, this means that hydrophobic modification can turn polyacrylamide from a flexible, shear-thinning aqueous polymer into a more structured, thickening material that is better suited to high-shear, high-salinity, and high-temperature environments [N1-R1][N5-F2]. But the same modification also makes the polymer more sensitive to water structure, ions, and concentration, so its behavior is not uniform across all aqueous conditions [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-F2].

Overall, hydrophobic side chains introduced through copolymerization do not simply add “fatty” groups to polyacrylamide; they reconfigure the polymer’s structure and solution behavior in a way that can be deliberately tuned for specific aqueous applications [N1-R1][N2-R1][N5-F2].

### 1) How hydrophobic side chains are introduced into polyacrylamide

Hydrophobic side chains are introduced through copolymerization, not post-functionalization. The branch report on mechanistic effects states that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide (HMPAM) is obtained through radical copolymerization of acrylamide with a hydrophobic monomer, and that hydrophobic monomers such as styrene are embedded in the polymer backbone during synthesis [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1]. The synthesis evidence also confirms that hydrophobic monomers are chemically incorporated into the copolymer chain, as shown by NMR and SEC characterization of HMPAM [N1-F1]. This is important because it means the hydrophobicity is intrinsic to the polymer structure, not a surface or end-group feature that can be easily removed.

### 2) How hydrophobic groups influence chain conformation and hydration

Hydrophobic side chains reduce the polymer’s compatibility with water and alter hydration and conformation. The branch report on structure and conformation says that the LCST of a polymer-water solution is related to the degree of hydrophobicity of the repeating unit, and that hydrophobic hydration can be experimentally evaluated in single polymers [N2-R1][N2-R2]. It also notes that the relaxation time of polymer-water hydrogen bonds increases with hydrophobicity, suggesting that hydrophobic groups disrupt hydrogen bonding and hydration [N2-R3]. This means the polymer chain becomes less extended and more compact as hydrophobicity increases, and that water molecules around the chain behave differently than they would around a purely hydrophilic chain.

In polyacrylamide, this effect is especially relevant because PAM is already a highly water-soluble polymer, and the branch report on context explains that hydrophobically modified polyacrylamide is introduced to improve properties such as tolerance to saline environments and shear resistance [N1-R1][N1-F1]. The same context report also notes that PAM is widely used in aqueous systems and is of particular interest in enhanced oil recovery because it can serve as a high-impact viscosity modifier [N5-F2]. That shows why hydrophobicity matters: even a small change in hydrophobic side chains can shift the polymer’s compatibility with water and change how it behaves in aqueous solution.
